lastText: GHQSITUATION REPORTHome19141915191619171918HARD MODE — EROSION 3/5-7MANPOWER-5MUNITIONS-1POLITICAL CAPITALXI.1918The Hundred DaysThe armistice comes into force at eleven in the morning. The British armies, which began the year holding the longest line in France and short of men, have ended it advancing on a broad front, with a large share of the prisoners and guns taken since August to their credit. The army that landed in August 1914 has been replaced several times over, and the Cabinet that sent it has been replaced twice. The argument between the generals and the politicians is not over, and will be carried on in print for the next twenty years.Settled recordLanding, August 1914: assembled at Amiens. The Seine, September 1914: the army kept to the line. Ypres, 1914: the line was held. The Dardanelles, March 1915: the 29th Division released. The shortage of shells: told to the press. Loos: attacked, with the reserve close behind. Gallipoli, November 1915: evacuated. December 1915: French kept for the winter. 1916: compulsion for single men. The Somme: a compromise plan, and a costly first day. The tanks: used on 15 September, and the surprise spent. Calais, February 1917: the subordination refused. Convoy: tried from May 1917. Flanders, 1917: authorised. January 1918: the line extended to Barisis. The general reserve: refused. Doullens: Foch accepted to coordinate. April 1918: a withdrawal in Flanders authorised. September 1918: the attacks continued against the Hindenburg
